title: My day
goal: Describe your daily routine, master the biggest verb type, and see that consonant gradation in verbs is actually very tidy: weak for I and you, strong for he and she.
bekal: conjugate type 1 verbs in full, including consonant gradation
link one verb to another: *haluan mennä*, *osaan puhua*, *voin tulla*
describe a whole day from waking up to going back to bed

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Arkipäivä
dialogs.intro: In class, the teacher asks everyone to describe an ordinary day. It's Budi's turn.

lines.speaker: Opettaja:
lines.text: Budi, kerro. Mitä sinä teet tavallisena päivänä?
lines.id: Budi, tell us. What do you do on an ordinary day?
lines.literal: Budi, tell. what you make as-ordinary as-day?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Minä herään seitsemältä. En nouse heti — luen puhelinta sängyssä.
lines.id: I wake up at seven. I don't get up right away — I read my phone in bed.
lines.literal: I wake from-seven. not-I rise at-once — read-I phone-some in-bed.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Syön puuroa ja juon kahvia. Sitten lähden bussilla kouluun.
lines.id: I eat porridge and drink coffee. Then I take the bus to school.
lines.literal: eat-I porridge-some and drink-I coffee-some. then leave-I by-bus to-school.

lines.speaker: Opettaja:
lines.id: How long does the trip take?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Puoli tuntia. Luen kirjaa bussissa, mutta usein nukun.
lines.id: Half an hour. I read a book on the bus, but I often fall asleep.
lines.literal: half hour-some. read-I book-some in-bus, but often sleep-I.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Teen töitä ravintolassa. Tulen kotiin yhdeksältä.
lines.id: I work in a restaurant. I get home at nine.
lines.literal: make-I work-plural-some in-restaurant. come-I to-home from-nine.

lines.speaker: Opettaja:
lines.text: Se on pitkä päivä. Milloin sinä opiskelet suomea?
lines.id: That's a long day. When do you study Finnish?
lines.literal: it is long day. when you study Finnish-some?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Illalla. Kirjoitan sanoja vihkoon ja katson suomalaista sarjaa.
lines.id: In the evening. I write words in my notebook and watch a Finnish series.
lines.literal: in-evening. write-I word-plural-some into-notebook and watch-I Finnish-some series-some.

lines.speaker: Opettaja:
lines.id: Excellent! Do you understand the series?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: En ymmärrä paljon. Mutta minä haluan oppia, ja se riittää.
lines.id: I don't understand much. But I want to learn, and that's enough.
lines.literal: not-I understand much. but I want learn, and it suffices.

notes: **Herään, but hän herää.** Notice the pattern that keeps coming back in the dialogue: the *minä* and *sinä* forms use the **weak** consonant, the *hän* form uses the **strong** one. *Luen* but *hän lukee*; *otan* but *hän ottaa*; *tiedän* but *hän tietää*. Once you see it as a pattern, hundreds of verbs become predictable.

**What you read and watch takes the partitive.** *Luen kirja**a***, *katson sarja**a***, *ymmärrätkö sarja**a***. The reason: reading a book is an ongoing activity, not finished. If you read the book to the end, the form changes: *luin kirja**n***. The full rule is in Unit 11.

**Teen töitä** literally means "I make works". Finnish has no everyday one-word verb for "to work" — there is *työskennellä*, but it sounds formal. The everyday phrase is *tehdä töitä*, always with the plural partitive *töitä*.

**Seitsemältä and yhdeksältä** — clock times take the ending *-lta/-ltä*, literally "from seven". Finnish sees the hour as a surface you pass over, not a point you sit on. Don't try to make sense of the logic; just learn the form. Telling the time in full comes in Unit 10.
**Bussilla kouluun** — two endings at once. *Bussi**lla*** = by bus (the means), *koulu**un*** = to school (the direction). These direction endings are the subject of the next unit.

**Haluan oppia** — the second verb stays in the dictionary form. After *haluta*, *osata*, *voida*, and their cousins, the next verb keeps its untouched dictionary form: *haluan **oppia***, *osaan **puhua***, *voin **tulla***. Just like English "I want to learn" — the second verb doesn't change.

grammars.title: Verb type 1
body: The biggest group and the one you'll meet most often: verbs whose dictionary form ends in **two different vowels** — *puhu-a*, *asu-a*, *luke-a*, *otta-a*, *tietä-ä*.
after: **The pattern in one sentence: weak for *minä*, *sinä*, *me*, *te* — strong for *hän* and *he*.** That's all. Four rows are the same, two rows (*hän*, *he*) keep the original consonant from the dictionary form.
*Puhua* and *asua* show nothing because they have no k/p/t to weaken. Most verbs of this type are actually like that, so don't assume everything changes.
⚠️ The *hän* form lengthens the last vowel: *puhu**u***, *luke**e***, *otta**a***. If the stem vowel is already long, nothing is added: *saa → hän saa*, not *saaa*.

grammars.title: Verbs that attach to verbs
body: Six very common verbs, all followed by the dictionary form — just like "want to" or "can" in English.

head: Verb
Meaning
Example
Translation
rows: to intend, to be going to
I'm going to go to Finland.

after: Only the **first** verb changes; the second stays as it is in the dictionary. *Haluan mennä*, *haluat mennä*, *hän haluaa mennä* — *mennä* never changes.
Negation also hits the first one: *en halua mennä*, *emme osaa uida*.

⚠️ *Haluta* and *osata* aren't actually type 1 — their *minä* forms are *haluan* and *osaan*, which you can't guess from the dictionary form. For now, learn these six as they are; their type is explained in Unit 12.

blocks.text: All the time expressions above use the ending **-lla/-llä**, which originally means "on a surface". Finnish pictures time as a surface we move across, not a container we step into. Note the gradation: *ilta → illalla*, *päivä → päivällä*.

Their position is fairly free, but the most natural spot is **after the subject and before the verb**: *Minä usein nukun bussissa* or *Usein nukun bussissa*. Putting it at the end is also correct and adds a little emphasis: *Nukun bussissa usein*.

blocks.title: Kuinka usein sinä…?
items: *Kuinka usein sinä käyt saunassa?* — How often do you go to the sauna?
*Kaksi kertaa viikossa.* — Twice a week. (a very Finnish answer)
*Kuinka kauan?* — How long? Don't mix it up with *kuinka usein* (how often).

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Joka* means "every", and the noun doesn't change: *joka päivä*, *joka viikko*, *joka aamu*. It is one of the few words that demands no ending at all — enjoy it while it lasts.
